panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Structural MRI of a DRS3 patient showing absence of the left abducens nerve, with the arrow indicating the normal right abducens nerve, a recognized imaging finding associated with Duane retraction syndrome. [raw subtype: DRS3] B: DTI MRI of the same DRS3 patient, with the arrow highlighting the normal right abducens nerve, confirming the absence of the left abducens nerve associated with the syndrome. [raw subtype: DRS3] C: DTI tractography of a DRS3 patient showing abnormal left corticospinal tract (failure to cross to the contralateral side) and absent projective fibers from abducens neurons to contralateral ocular motor neurons via the medial longitudinal fasciculus, associated imaging findings in this subtype of Duane retraction syndrome. [raw subtype: DRS3]

in_text_mentions: The abducens nerve was absent in 12 of the 14 patients with DRS1, including the patients with the CHN1 and SALL4 gene mutations, and 9 of the 17 with DRS3 in MRI images. Hypoplasia of the abducens nerve was observed in four patients with DRS2 (Figure 3). In addition, the projective fibers from the abducens neurons to the contralateral ocular motor neurons via the medial longitudinal fasciculus were also absent in those patients without abducens nerve in the DTI images (Figure 4).

in_text_mentions: n abnormal head posture. Her palpebral fissures were normal and equal on both sides in the primary position of gaze. panels.figure_caption: Digital face photographs of the patient demonstrating (a) orthotropia with right face turn, (b1) left eye exotropia in forced primary position when fixing with the right eye, (b2) increase in the deviation while fixing with the left eye, (c) absence of convergence, (d–l) ocular movements in cardinal positions of gaze.
in_text_mentions: Orthoptic examination (Figure 1) was significant for a 20-degree right side face turn with which she had orthotropia for the near and distance. In forced primary position, she had a 20-degree exotropia in the left eye. The exotropia was 45 degrees while fixing with the left eye. The exotropia increased in upgaze and reduced in downgaze (V pattern). Abduction and adduction in the left eye were limited. The extraocular movements in the right eye were normal. There was no globe retraction, palpebral fissure changes, upshoot or downshoot in the left eye. Convergence was absent.

in_text_mentions: upshoot. Right eye hypotropia was increased from 5 PD in the primary position to 25 PD in the upward gaze. A slightly positive FDT accompanied the right eye’s limitation of elevation. Bell’s phenomenon was also significantly lower in the right eye. Palpebral fissure height was symmetric on both sides in the inferior gaze. The horizontal deviation was 12 PD of exotropia in both superior and inferior gazes, and no pattern was detected. At the time of examination, the Bielschowsky head tilt test did not make any changes in the examination, and no compensatory face turn was observed (Fig. 1 A-E).
